messages.content: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month.

response:
The Moon appears to change shape over the course of a month because the Sun illuminates different portions of the Moon's face as the Moon orbits the Earth. The Moon does not produce its own light — what we see from Earth is the side of the Moon that is facing us reflecting sunlight. As the Moon moves around the Earth, different portions of it are turned toward the Sun at any given time, causing different fractions of the Moon to be illuminated.

Specifically, when the Moon is on one side of Earth relative to the Sun (first quarter), we see half the Moon lit up. As the Moon moves further around Earth, more of its far side begins to face the Sun and more of its near side faces away, producing the shape we call three-quarters full. At full moon, the side of the Moon facing Earth is fully illuminated. As the Moon continues its orbit, the fraction of the Moon that is lit from Earth's perspective gradually decreases again, passing through third quarter and half moon shapes until it returns to new moon, when the side of the Moon facing Earth is not illuminated at all by the Sun.

This apparent shape change is known as the lunar cycle or the moon phases, and it repeats approximately every 29.5 days, which is the length of a lunar month.

response: To compare two fractions, find a common denominator — the smallest number that both denominators divide into evenly. Multiply the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the number that will make its denominator match the common denominator. Once the denominators are the same, the fraction with the larger numerator is greater. If the numerators are equal, the fractions are equivalent. For example, to compare 3/4 and 5/6, use 12 as the common denominator (4 x 3 = 12 and 6 x 2 = 12). This gives you 9/12 and 10/12. Since 10 is greater than 9, 5/6 is greater than 3/4.

response: A metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one in the same room mainly because metal is a better thermal conductor than wood. Conductors move heat energy quickly through their material — so when you hold the metal spoon, that heat quickly transfers from your hand to the metal, and some of it escapes into the air from the exposed end. Wood, being a poorer conductor, retains more of the heat coming from your hand and stays warmer to the touch. The room temperature is the same for both, but your sensory impression is driven by which material is more efficient at losing heat. This is why kitchen tools like spoons and forks are often metal — they quickly reach the cold or hot temperature of the food you're handling, giving you an accurate reading.
